content.title: Interesting and well motivated paper on the transferability of fairness between train and test data when the distribution shift is due to missing values in the training set.
content.review:
#### Summary:

This paper addressed the problem of transferability of fairness between train and test data that have different distributions. They specifically focus on the case where the difference is due to the presence of missing values in the training data while the test data contains full observations. The authors make the distinction between “complete case domain” which represents the training data where observations with missing values are discarded versus “complete data domain” in which there are no missing values and represents the test / real data. 

They propose to evaluate, on the complete data case, the fairness of a model trained to achieve some group fairness constraints on a training data with missing values (complete case domain). They focus on the “accuracy parity gap” (\delta) measure they introduce as the difference in prediction error for two different demographic groups. The objective is to correctly estimate \delta_T on the complete data domain (realistic test set, subscript T) from \delta_S in the complete case domain (training set with extracted fully observed examples, subscript S). 

The proposed approach is based on weighting the fully observed examples in the training set in computing the prediction error. They provide a lower and upper bound on |\delta_T  -  \delta_S^hat| and analyse them for the different possible missingness mechanisms on the training set.

#### Strengths:

- The paper addresses an important problem that is not yet fully explored, which can be useful to the algorithmic fairness literature
- The authors provide an in-depth theoretical analysis of the proposed fairness estimator which extends upon prior work on transferability of fairness between different domains. However, I have not checked the provided proofs in detail.
- The paper is well written and theoretical results are discussed and analysed through experiments on both synthetic ans real data. 

#### Weaknesses:

The definition of Z_obs and Z_mis are unclear. The complete case domain is defined as the subsampling fully observed examples for training to circumvent missing data in the training set. The work assesses how the fairness differs in the complete data domain  for a model trained on the complete case domain. Section 2.2 defines the training set for the predictor as Z_obs. However, the definition of Z_obs section 2.1 corresponds to selecting the observed features for each example in the training.

#### Recommendation:

I recommend acceptance for this paper. I believe this paper addresses an interesting problem which is not extensively explored in the literature, as far as I know. The work is theoretically well motivated and the authors do a good job of clearly discussing the different implications of the missingness mechanism on the results. 

#### Questions:

Clarify the definition of Z_obs and Z_miss in terms of D_S and D_T

#### Additional feedback:
1) The nomenclature “complete case” vs “complete data” is not very distinctive. I would recommend finding better names that clearly distinguishes the two notions.
2) Typos: 
- Last paragraph in section 1.1: cross → across
- Line 4 in section 2.1: ‘define’ → ‘we define’
- Line 4 in section 2.1: 1{z_{ij} is observed} → 1_{z_{ij} is observed} 
- Line 5 in section 2.1: ‘Denote” → ‘We denote’
- Last line, paragraph 2, section 2.1: ‘fairness guarantee’ → ‘fairness guarantees’ or ‘a fairness guarantee’
- Line 2, paragraph 3, section 2.1: 1{z_i is fully observed} → 1_{z_i is fully observed}
content.confidence: 3: The reviewer is fairly confident that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Application of a classic method on a metric motivated by fairness
content.review:
The paper studies a fairness metric that captures the difference between the average accuracy of a predictor among the two classes of a protected binary attribute. This is a natural metric of group fairness, and the paper is devoted to the study of the following question: how can we estimate this metric when the distribution of the data points we have is different from the real distribution (perhaps through a mechanism that removes some of the data points in a way that potentially correlates with the protected attribute). 

The solution is to simply apply the generic propensity score matching technique: when the distribution of available data is different from the real distribution, to estimate an estimand with respect to the real distribution simply weigh each data point by the inverse of its propensity score. The paper proves bounds on the accuracy of this method. The bound is composed of two parts, the first capturing how different the weights are from true inverse propensity scores, and the second is the sampling error, which is roughly between O(1/sqrt(n)) and O(sqrt(log(n)/n)), where n is the size of the smaller class. This estimation method is then evaluated empirically on a number of data sets.

On the positive side, the paper is well-written and easy to read, the model, the fairness metric, and the methods are all reasonable, and the results make sense. On the negative side, there's really not much technical novelty. The paper simply applies a well-known method on an estimand that happens to be defined to capture fairness, and the results are simple applications of classic bounds on this estimand. For this reason, I don't think the paper meets the acceptance bar for ICLR.
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection

content.title: Response to Reviewer 2
content.comment:
Thank you for your thoughtful and constructive comments! We provide our response to your concerns below:

We would like to highlight four novel contributions in this work. First, the paper provides new insights for the algorithmic fairness in learning tasks when datasets contain missing values, which, to the best of our knowledge, has not yet been investigated from a theoretical perspective. Second, we characterize the role and impact of the missing data mechanism on correction for the data domain shift in fairness estimation for analysis of incomplete data.  Third, there has been limited theoretical work on domain adaptation problems when estimated weights are used to correct for domain shift. Cortes et al. (2010) considers the setting where true weights are known, Swaminathan & Joachims (2015) considers the case when weights are estimated, but their analysis of algorithm’s generalization performance is compared with a clipped empirical risk and does not provide any lower bound. In this work we investigated the setting where the weights are estimated from the data based on correctly or incorrectly specified propensity score models under a given missing data mechanism. Besides, both upper and lower bounds for fairness estimation bias are provided. Fourth, while the estimand that is of primary interest in domain adaptation literature is prediction accuracy, the estimand of our interests takes the form of difference between two prediction accuracy terms. As a result, the form of the lower bound in our work is somewhat different from the form of the lower bound in the existing works.

content.title: The paper talks about convergence bounds for incomplete data case but lacks novelty and insight. The method also seems impractical.
content.review:
The paper presents an IPS weighted estimator for fairness using the accuracy parity gap. The contribution of the paper lies in proposing the IPS estimator that operates on the complete rows of the data with weights that can be estimated by fitting a propensity model. The paper then provides convergence guarantees for the estimator in addition to experiments on simulations show how the method is effective.

Although the proven bounds in the paper are rigorous, I still do not consider the contributions of the paper to be significantly novel to merit an acceptance for the following reasons: 
1. The paper extends the already well-studied theory of importance sampling for unbiased estimation (and learning which this paper doesn't touch) from Cortes et al. 2010, and more recently Swaminathan & Joachims 2015. Just like the authors argue that the convergence bounds "can similarly be derived for other fairness metrics", the bounds for accuracy parity gap proposed in this paper can itself be derived from the references above. 
2. I believe that it is important to study the case of missing data in the context of fairness in machine learning but using a method that ignores data rows (with missing values) is far from desirable. Given that the paper proposes a method that only uses the rows with complete data for fitting the model and the learnt model is only usable for prediction a complete row. From an application perspective, even though through a certifiable method one can verify that the model is fair according to a particular metric, the model may already have suffered from underfitting because of all the data that is dropped. Even though this doesn't show up in the convergence rates, it is indeed an effect when working with finite data. 
3. The choice of propensity models in the experiments section seems to be crafted to the needs of the model: If we were to tune the propensity model in the experiments section to have an order of magnitude higher propensity of missingness, only a very few data points will have all the columns available. This is indeed a problem as it makes the method unusable.
4. There are a plethora of other--more prevalent--methods that are used to handle missing data e.g. imputation-based methods, that are not studied in the paper. 
5. Minor: In the experiments section, It is not clear what "missing values are generated using the propensity model..." means. Perhaps it should mean the missingness of data (or the random value for observation) is drawn using the propensity model?
6. One of the drawbacks of IPS methods that rely on predicting IPS scores is model misspecification (as also mentioned in the paper). The results in the case of using predicted propensities are not explained enough. It is not clear why everything except Random Forest would behave like the uniform propensity model. As far as I understand, the more expressive the propensity model class is, the more likely it is to be able to model the true propensity. So XGBoost if used correctly should at least be as good as RF. Also, some works show that it is not even necessary for the propensity model to be very accurate for the debiasing using IPS to work very well (for example Schnable et al. 2016 (Recommendations as Treatments...)).
content.confidence: 4: The reviewer is confident but not absolutely certain that the evaluation is correct

content.title: Response to Reviewer 1 [Part 2/2]
content.comment:
**C5: Writing**

Yes the sentence means that the missingness of the data is generated from the postulated propensity model.

**C6: Experimental results**

Effect of model misspecification can be viewed from the results under MNAR mechanisms in two real datasets, in which weights other than true weights are given by misspecified propensity score models. Fairness estimators using true weights have smaller bias. In both real and synthetic datasets, correctly specified propensity score models (logistic models) also result in smaller estimation bias compared to other propensity score models.
 The true propensity score of an observation is the probability of observing all variables in the observation, which is a real number between 0 and 1. In addition, due to the positivity assumption typically made in the missing data literature, the true propensity score is bounded away from 0. On the other hand, the training samples used to fit the propensity score model has only binary labels (0 for missing data and 1 for missing and observed data). A more expressive model such as XGBoost is more likely to predict the label 1 for observed data and 0 for missing data, but it does NOT always lead to more accurate estimation of the true propensity score. Actually when a XGBoost model yields perfect prediction of the label for observed data (1) with the predicted probability close to 1 for all complete cases, then the resulting weights for all complete cases would be close to 1which would be very similar to uniform propensity scores. It follows that the results using propensity scores estimated from XGBoost would be similar to those using the uniform propensity scores.

content.title: Response to Reviewer 1 [Part 1/2]
content.comment:
Thank you for your thoughtful and constructive comments! We provide point-by-point responses to your concerns below:

**C1: Derivation of bounds**

While the estimand that is of primary interest in domain adaptation literature is prediction accuracy, the estimand of our interest takes the form of difference between two prediction accuracy terms. While the upper bound we obtain can be derived along the lines of existing work in domain adaptation, the derivation of the lower bound is more nuanced. In particular, in the proof of Theorem 2, proper relaxations after applying Bernstein’s inequalities are required in order to obtain the results, which does not appear in existing works that study lower bound in domain adaptation problems such as Cortes et al. (2010). As a result, the form of the lower bound in our work is somewhat different from the form of the lower bound in the existing works.
We would like to highlight three additional contributions in this work. First, the paper provides new insights for the algorithmic fairness in learning tasks when datasets contain missing value, which, to the best of our knowledge, has not yet been investigated from a theoretical perspective.  Second, we characterize the role and impact of the missing data mechanism on correction for the data domain shift  in fairness estimation for incomplete data. Third, there has been limited theoretical work on domain adaptation problems when estimated weights are used to correct for domain shift. While existing works such as Cortes et al. (2010) consider the case where the true weights are known, we investigated an additional setting where the weights are estimated from the data based on correctly or incorrectly specified propensity score models under a given missing data mechanism. Of note, in Swaminathan & Joachims (2015), the generalization performance of importance sampling is compared with a clipped empirical risk while we consider the empirical risk without truncations. The corresponding proof techniques are different from this work. Besides, there is no lower bound in Swaminathan & Joachims (2015).

**C2: Concerns for complete case analysis**

We would like to clarify that the goal of this paper is NOT to propose using weighted complete cases for analysis of incomplete data. We recognize that there are other more powerful methods for handling missing data such as  imputation and our work takes the first step into theoretically assessing fairness for learning tasks in the presence of missing data. It lays the foundation for future research on assessing fairness for other methods for analysis of incomplete data, since to our knowledge, there has been no work in this area yet.

**C3: PS models in experiments**

We agree that in some situations, most of the observations (rows) have missing values. In such cases, indeed it may be impractical to use the complete-case analysis. Again, we want to re-emphasize the points made in our previous response.

**C4: Analysis of missing data imputation**

Again, our work takes the first step into theoretically assessing fairness for learning tasks in the presence of missing data and lays the foundation for future research on assessing fairness for other more powerful methods such as imputation for analysis of incomplete data, since to our knowledge, there has been no work in this area yet. In addition, there are some potential challenges when studying imputation-based methods. Fairness for analysis of imputed data would depend on the specific imputation method used, as different imputation methods may have different operating characteristics and theoretical properties. If we adopt the same strategy of domain adaptation, then we need to know the distribution of  imputed data (domain) in comparison with the distribution of the complete data (domain). However, properties of imputed data distribution for many of the popular imputation methods still remain unknown or under-investigated. For example, theoretical properties of popular deep learning imputation methods such as Mida (Gondara et al. 2018), Gain (Yoon et al. 2018) and misGan (Li et al. 2019) have not been studied. Theoretical properties of multiple imputation via chain equations (MICE, Buuren et al. 2010) and missForest (Stekhoven et al. 2012) have not been well-established except for some very restrictive settings. Matrix completion methods (e.g. Mazumder et al. 2010) are only investigated regarding their imputation errors, but not for imputed data distribution.

display_title: Important Topic that Merits Further Study. Rigorous Theoretical Analysis with Unclear Value in Practice.

content.title: Important Topic that Merits Further Study. Rigorous Theoretical Analysis with Unclear Value in Practice.
content.review:
# Summary

This paper presents a theoretical analysis of the estimation error of group fairness metrics in settings with missing data. The authors consider standard mechanisms that result in missing data and derive an upper bound and a lower bound on the estimation error for classification and regression problems. The paper includes numerical experiments on synthetic and real datasets to illustrate the tightness of each bound.

# Pros

- Paper focuses on an understudied topic that is relevant to many practical applications of machine learning.

- Versatile theoretical analysis that applies to different fairness metrics as well as classification and regression problems. The paper includes a lower bound, which seems noteworthy, and could guide future theoretical work in this setting.

- Paper includes experiments, which is appreciated in a theory paper. In particular, the experiments on the ADNI dataset seem well-suited for this setting and should be a focus of any future on this topics.

# Cons / Comments

- Paper does not illustrate or motivate practical issues that may arise as a result of incomplete data. This seems like a missed opportunity as it is one of the only works focusing on this topic. The paper would be far stronger if the authors could clearly describe some of the failure modes due to missingness. 

- The practical value of the upper and lower bounds is unclear. Both bounds depend on quantities that are difficult to estimate from data (e.g., propensity scores or the total variation distance between distributions).  The upper bound is likely to be vacuous in most settings where we would care about fairness. 

- The experimental results provide minimal added value. In particular, the "quality" of the bounds (i.e., the main result that would justify the bounds) are only assessed through experiments on synthetic data. The results of this experiment are extremely difficult to parse. The experiment focuses on a regression task, does not normalize the estimation error,  and reports the bais on a log-scale.

- Ideally, the experiments on synthetic data should focus on a classification task, which is far more relevant to the fairness literature. The paper would be *far* stronger if the authors could report estimation bias in a way that would be accessible to a general audience. 

# Rating

Overall, the paper considers an important problem but does not address it in a way that will have a long-term impact. My main concerns are that: (1) the paper does not describe the issues related to missingness in a way that is accessible to a general audience; (2) the main contributions of the paper (i.e., the upper and lower bound) appear to have limited practical value. 

Given these reasons, I have currently awarded the paper a 4. However, I am willing to *dramatically* raise my score if the authors were to report results for a synthetic dataset for a classification problem in a way that would be accessible to a general audience (as this could address both of my concerns).  To this end, the results that I am looking for is a statement like the following:

"We consider a synthetic classification dataset where the true performance disparity between groups A and B is 10%. In this problem, we find that our estimates of the disparity gap vary between 8% to 12% when we sample n = 5000 points from each group with no missingness. These estimates vary between  -5% to 15% when there is missingness (suggesting that we can incorrectly evaluate fairness X% of the time). Using the bounds provided in this work, we know that – with probability at least 95% – the estimates of the disparity gap will range between -10% to 20%. This is useful because..."
content.rating: 4: Ok but not good enough - rejection

content.title: Response to Reviewer 3
content.comment:
Thank you for your thoughtful and constructive comments! We provide point-by-point responses to your concerns below:

**C1: Practical issue of fairness due to missingness**

Here is one example to illustrate the practical issues as a result of incomplete data. Suppose personal information along with annual income is asked in a questionnaire which is administered to a random sample of people selected from the target population of interest. If people with low income are less likely to report their income, this would cause a higher proportion of missing information in this subgroup. Suppose income level is associated with gender. We train a model for predicting income using observed data. Even if this model is trained using observed data to be fair with respect to gender, it may not be fair in the complete data domain, i.e., for the target population. Additionally, such failure mode can also been viewed from experiments of two real datasets in the paper. Using propensity score as weights for fairness estimation, as suggested, can reduce about 30% of the bias compared with using uniform weights, i.e. analysis of incomplete data without reweighting.


**C2: Practical value of bounds**

The main message from both of the bounds is about quantifying the convergence rates which can provide valuable insights and guidance in practice. For example, the order of the convergence rates of the upper and lower bounds can help understand the impact of the sample size and guide choosing adequate sample size in practice,  In addition, if the weights used in fairness estimation are not close to the true propensity score weights, it would be difficult to guarantee that the total variation distance term in the upper bound will vanish. Therefore, if we wish to guarantee fairness, proper weights should be adopted in fairness estimation. The lower bound is more information-theoretic as it does not need assumptions on the learning algorithm. At a high level, it indicates that even when true weights are known and adopted, with some non-zero probability, the order of fairness estimation bias will be no better than $\mathcal{O}(n^{-1/2})$, regardless of the algorithm.


**C3: Experimental results**

In the experiments, we firstly justify the effectiveness of lower bound, then explore the effect of several factors on the fairness estimation. We anticipate such results to inspire future work to systematically study the effect of those factors. Two real datasets are also used to compare the fairness estimation using different weights.
We would also like to clarify that if the response is not normalized in the regression task, the upper and lower bound will also hold with some minor modification (see Remarks 1 and 3 in Section 3). The plots are shown in log scale so that the corresponding convergence rate (regarding sample size) can be clearly viewed from the curves’ slopes.

**C4: Experiments on classification tasks**

Some follow-up experiments on classification will appear in the updated version.

content.title: Some nice work; some lack of clarity (which may or may not be due to my own lack of background)
content.review:
Summary: This paper gives theoretical guarantees on the “accuracy parity gap” – difference between accuracies on two sensitive groups – under a missing data condition. They give an upper + lower bound with analysis of convergence, and also provide some experimental validation of their results.

Recommendation: Due to my lack of clarity on the communication of the problem, I lean reject for this paper. However, my confidence is low due to my lack of in-depth theoretical knowledge (i.e. not an expert in generalization bounds) in this area.

Strengths:
-	Theoretical work seems sound (although I am not an expert in the theory-heavy side of this)
-	This type of fairness metric is interesting, and doesn’t receive much attention I find
-	Empirical explorations of sample imbalance and model misspecification are useful

Weaknesses + Clarifications:
-	I am a little confused about the definition of “missing data”. The authors seem to define it through D_S, which is the set of examples where no component is missing. If this is the case, then why even bother with missing components at all in the problem model? We could equivalently consider it a form of dataset shift – either a point is present, or it is not
-	In general, the motivation needs work – not quite clear how this should map onto real scenarios. For instance, top of 2.3 “fairness in the complete data domain is of primary interest” – it isn’t quite clear why this is true
-	More analysis of the missingness mechanisms would be nice as they are discussed in detail at the top 
-	Would like to see more clarification of the difference between this paper and Martinez-Plumed (2019) – you don’t really touch on it in 1.2
-	In Theorem 2, I’m not sure how to interpret “with probability at least 7 / 1440” – this seems very low. Is this a useful result in this case? My interpretation is that this result relies on there existing potentially a very odd sample, which doesn’t seem like such a useful thing to know. However I might be misunderstanding results of this type
-	Additionally, my confusion propagates in Fig 1a – is there some intuition for why this bound might work despite this possibly very low probability of holding? Would like some intuition

Other feedback:
-	The motivation section in the intro needs some work – would be good to focus more on the specific examples in the second paragraph.
-	Top of 2.1 – z_(0)I definition is confusing. Does this mean a certain number of “missing” tokens? The elements which are actually unobserved? The indices which have missing data?
-	Why is D_T called a domain if it is a distribution? 
-	Top of 3.2 – how can the bound on the variance be shown? Not obvious to me
-	In COMPAS experiment design – why does it matter which feature you throw out? My understanding is that if any feature is missing, the whole data point is removed from the complete case domain and as such is a “missing” data point
content.confidence: 2: The reviewer is willing to defend the evaluation, but it is quite likely that the reviewer did not understand central parts of the paper

content.title: Response to Reviewer 5
content.comment:
Thank you for your thoughtful and constructive comments! We provide point-by-point responses to your concerns below:


**C1: Definition of "missing data"**

There are a number of approaches to handle missing data, among which the complete-case analysis that uses only observations/cases with all variables fully observed is one of the widely used approaches in practice due to its ease of use. The domain of complete cases is defined as $\mathcal{D}_S$. Indeed we can consider that there is a domain shift from $\mathcal{D}_S$ to $\mathcal{D}_T$. This shift in the setting of incomplete data can be characterized by the true propensity score. To mitigate the fairness estimation bias caused by the shift, weights are adopted in the fairness estimator. As indicated in the manuscript,missing data mechanism plays a vital role in obtaining the ‘’right’’ weight. For MCAR, uniform weights are equivalent to the true weights. For MAR, one can train popular nonparametric models to obtain a consistent estimator for the true weights. For MNAR, it’s much more difficult to obtain consistent estimators for the true weights. Hence one of our contributions is to characterize the role and impact of the missing data mechanism on correction for the data domain shift in fairness estimation for analysis of incomplete data.


**C2: Motivation**

In many biomedical studies, samples in the complete data domain are considered to be randomly drawn from the target population for which we are interested in assessing fairness; in other words, the complete data domain is defined by the target population. Under MAR and MNAR, the complete case domain, however, is biased for estimation of fairness in the complete data domain, i.e., for the target population. 
Here is one example to illustrate this point. Suppose personal information along with annual income is asked in a questionnaire which is administered to a random sample of people selected from the target population of interest. If people with low income are less likely to report their income, this would cause a higher proportion of missing information in this subgroup. Suppose income level is associated with gender. We train a model for predicting income using observed data. Even if this model is trained using observed data and is fair with respect to gender (on observed data), it may not be fair in the complete data domain. 

**C3: Analysis of the missingness mechanisms**

More analysis of missing data mechanisms will appear in the updated version.


**C4: Difference with Martinez-Plumed (2019)**

The key difference between our work and Martinez et al. (2019) is the object in analysis. They empirically evaluate the fairness of data analysis after missing data imputation, while we provide theoretical guarantees on fairness in the analysis of incomplete data.

**C5: Probability in the lower bound**

The bounds are established under weak conditions on data distributions. For those with light tail behaviors (e.g. sub-gaussian tail), such probability would be relatively tight. If one is willing to make additional assumptions on the tail behavior (e.g. fat-tailed distribution), this probability can be even larger. We also note that the low probability in the lower bound of generalization error is not uncommon in the existing literature (e.g. Cortes et al. 2010, kontorovich et al. 2017). Meanwhile, to the best of our knowledge, there is fairly limited recent work on establishing lower bounds in this area.

**C6: About Figure-1**

As noted in our response to the previous comment,  the low probability, 7/1440, is a result of minimal assumptions about the tail behavior of the distribution. However, for certain distributions with a well-behaved tail distribution such as the case in our synthetic experiments,  the bound actually works with higher probability.

**Feedback 1**
We will add them in the updated version.

**Feedback 2**
$z_{(0),i}$ represents the missing components in sample $z_i$.

**Feedback 3**
By our definition, domain is equivalent to distribution and we use two terms interchangeably.

**Feedback 4**
Notice that $\omega$ is upper bounded by $B$ and the predicted and true responses are inside the unit interval, the bound comes from Popoviciu's inequality on variances.

**Feedback 5**
It’s really not important which feature was thrown out. We chose a specific model and a specific missing data mechanism for generating missing values because we think that it would be easier for readers to understand.

content.title: Missing data conception
content.comment: Thanks for the response. I still have some confusion around the way you're defining missing data. Why would we be referring to "generating missing values for the last feature" if the point is either included or removed entirely from D_S based on the missingness of the feature - why wouldn't we just say "we chose which points to remove from D_S"?

content.title: About missing data definition
content.comment: We define concrete missing data mechanisms instead of directly specifying complete cases (rows) as it will affect the estimation process of propensity scores. To be more specific, we use those features that do not have any missing values in any cases to train a predictor and obtain the estimated propensity scores. Different missing mechanisms, although might result in the same set of complete cases, will lead to different fairness estimation bias in the experiments.
